title: Calibration Drift in Low-Cost Particulate Matter Sensors Deployed Across an Urban Monitoring Network

headings.text: Calibration Drift in Low-Cost Particulate Matter Sensors Deployed Across an Urban Monitoring Network

key_sentences: Low-cost optical sensors have made dense air-quality monitoring affordable, but their readings drift as the instruments age.
We recommend scheduled recalibration instead of fixed replacement cycles.
Cities increasingly rely on networks of inexpensive particulate matter sensors to map exposure at the scale of a single street.
This paper addresses that gap with an eighteen-month field comparison.
The network consisted of 84 sensors of two models installed at 28 sites between March 2024 and August 2025.
We fitted the coefficients by ordinary least squares and report b as the drift rate.
Rates were highest at roadside sites, where dust loading is greatest, and lowest at park sites.
Averaged over all units, recalibration against the nearest reference removed 78 percent of the accumulated error after twelve months.
A fixed replacement cycle discards units whose readings can still be corrected, whereas scheduled recalibration keeps them in service at a fraction of the cost.
Scheduled recalibration against a nearby reference is a cheaper and more reliable way to keep low-cost networks usable than replacing units on a fixed cycle.
